opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way to understand machine-learning robotics today is that it isn't one field. It's several research traditions that grew up separately, each with its own instincts about what the hard problem is, and they're now crashing into each other.

The first lineage is classical robotics: control theory, motion planning, state estimation, mechanics. Those people think in models. You write down the dynamics, you reason about contact, stability, and constraints, and you get guarantees. Their great strength is rigor and an intuition for physics. Their weakness, historically, was that the world is messier than any model you can write down, especially for manipulation, where contact is discontinuous and objects are deformable and unknown.

The second lineage is reinforcement learning, which came partly from the control and optimization world and partly from the AI and games community. The instinct there is: don't hand-design the behavior, define a reward and let the system discover it. That gave us a lot of excitement, especially sim-to-real locomotion, where quadrupeds and humanoids trained in massively parallel simulation now walk and recover remarkably well. But RL has struggled with long-horizon manipulation, partly because reward design is hard and partly because simulating contact-rich interaction faithfully is still difficult.

The third lineage, and the one driving the current wave, comes from computer vision and large-scale learning. The belief is that data and scale win: collect lots of demonstrations, through teleoperation or other interfaces, train a big policy with imitation learning, and lean on pretrained vision-language models for semantics and generalization. That's where vision-language-action models, diffusion policies, and the "robot foundation model" framing come from. It has given us a real jump in how general and robust manipulation looks, but it tends to treat physics as something the data will implicitly cover, and it runs into the fact that robot data is expensive and much scarcer than text or images.

What I find most interesting is the boundaries between these camps. Each one has blind spots that another one fills. The learning people are rediscovering why contact, compliance, and hardware design matter. The classical people are realizing that models alone don't scale to open-world variety. And the RL people sit in the middle, asking how you get beyond imitation, how a robot improves itself rather than just copying humans.

So my view is that the next real progress probably won't come from any single lineage winning. It'll come from synthesis: learned policies that respect physical structure, data collection designed together with hardware, and learning methods that use demonstrations to get started and then use real-world experience to improve. The field is young enough that the people who can speak more than one of these languages have a real advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to see it is as several lineages that grew up mostly separately and are now colliding, sometimes productively and sometimes awkwardly.

The oldest one is classical robotics: control theory, kinematics, motion planning, state estimation. That tradition is deeply skeptical of anything that can't be analyzed. It gave us stable controllers, SLAM, and the whole idea that you should model the world and reason about it explicitly. Its weakness has always been perception and the long tail of messy, unstructured environments. Models break when the world doesn't match them.

Then there's the reinforcement-learning lineage, which really came into robotics through the deep RL wave around 2015 and onward. The intuition there is that you shouldn't hand-design behavior, you should let the system discover it through trial and error. That gave us remarkable results in simulation and in locomotion, where sim-to-real transfer actually works, because you can simulate contact dynamics reasonably well. But it struggled with manipulation and with sample efficiency, and a lot of the field quietly moved away from pure online RL for real robots.

The third lineage is imitation learning and the broader data-driven approach, which I'd argue is dominant right now. The bet is that the lesson from language and vision applies to robots too: collect large, diverse demonstration data, train big models, and let scale do the work. Behavior cloning, diffusion policies, and the vision-language-action models all sit in this camp. It inherited a lot of its culture from computer vision and NLP people who entered robotics, and they brought a very different set of instincts, more about datasets and benchmarks and less about guarantees.

And then there's a quieter lineage from computer vision and 3D perception, which is where I personally spent a lot of time. Pose estimation, scene understanding, correspondence. For a while that work felt like it was getting absorbed into end-to-end learning, but it keeps coming back, because robots still need to know where things are in space.

What I find interesting is that the current moment is not really one lineage winning. The big foundation-model efforts borrow the data philosophy from vision and language, but they still lean on classical control at the lowest level, because nobody wants a neural network running the servo loop at a kilohertz. RL is reappearing as a fine-tuning stage on top of imitation-trained policies rather than as the starting point. And simulation, which was the RL community's tool, is now being repurposed as a data generator for the imitation people.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say the field spent a decade arguing about which paradigm was right, and the honest answer turned out to be that each lineage solved a different layer of the problem. The real research question now is how these layers compose, and who gets to own the interfaces between them.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to see today’s machine-learning robotics as a meeting point of several research traditions. One comes from control: how do you make a physical system behave reliably under uncertainty? Another comes from robotics itself, with its emphasis on geometry, planning, and the relationship between sensing and action. And another comes from machine learning, where the question is how much of that behavior can be learned from experience rather than specified by hand.

Those traditions bring different instincts. A control researcher may ask about stability. A learning researcher may ask about generalization. A roboticist may ask what happens when the camera moves or the gripper slips. They’re all asking essential questions, but they don’t always use the same language or measure progress in the same way.

To me, the interesting work is at those intersections. Learning can give us flexibility, while control and physical structure can give us useful constraints. The challenge is figuring out which parts of a system should be learned, which should be built in, and how to make the combination work outside the conditions where it was developed.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to see several overlapping lineages. One comes from control theory: stability, feedback, system identification, and the idea that intelligence has to work in a closed loop. Another comes from classical robotics, with its emphasis on geometry, planning, state estimation, and explicit models. Then there’s the machine-learning lineage, which asks how much of that structure we can learn from experience instead of specifying by hand.

Even within learning, there are different instincts. Reinforcement learning emphasizes interaction and consequences; imitation learning emphasizes learning from demonstrations; representation learning emphasizes extracting useful structure from large amounts of data. Those instincts lead to different choices about what data to collect and what success should look like.

What interests me is where these traditions meet. A robot can have a very capable learned policy and still need careful feedback, uncertainty estimation, and a recovery strategy. So I don’t see progress as one lineage replacing the others. I see it as learning which assumptions we can relax, which structures remain useful, and how to combine them in a system that works beyond a carefully arranged demonstration.
